1.pericope_label: The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose... Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the chapter a contrast between the desolation of the chief enemy and the renewed beauty of Israel's inheritance, takes the three opening nouns for three degrees in the absence of culture, would render the flower the narcissus though primrose and crocus have both been proposed, sets the three names of cultivated beauty against the three of desolation, and observes that over this land will shine not the common light of day but the glory of the Lord. On the charge to strengthen weak hands he reasons that since the New Testament quotes the clause figuratively the words here are figurative too, and he connects the encouragement with the words a king of Judah used in the same crisis, king and prophet alike grounding their comfort in the righteousness of God's government. Delitzsch weighs the same three flowers: one ancient paraphrase gives the narcissus while the paraphrase here leaves the word indefinite as lilies, and the name itself points to a bulbous plant, probably the crocus and primrose, which were classed together and may easily be confounded, whereas narcissus and primrose have nothing in common except that both grow from bulbs.

Gill glosses the fearful heart as the hasty heart, belonging to men ready to fly from the enemy and inconsiderate of the promises, and assigns the charge about weak hands to the prophet. Calvin describes the change as God's own work, since he waters some parts of the earth more bountifully than others and afterwards withdraws the blessing for men's ingratitude, and passes by what he calls the dreams of the Jewish expositors, who apply every such passage to a temporal reign of the Messiah. On the doubled verb he offers two readings, either unbroken vegetation, so that the land shall not flower with a fading blossom and sink back into its old foulness but bloom continually, or the daily increase of improvement, since Christ adds to his grace in us from day to day; and on the charge to the weak he says the next verse shows the passage to concern the ministers of the word, the charge being seasonable since so many tokens of God's anger could not but fill even the strongest minds with alarm.

Clarke holds that the images are so consolatory and sublime that they oblige us to extend their fulfilment to the period when the Messiah shall take his great power and reign, since two verses were literally accomplished by our Saviour and his apostles but the context makes plain those miracles were not the whole import; he works the text hard, reporting that for one word the Greek read another and rendered it the deserts of Jordan, and that two scholars proposed the banks of Jordan. Wesley makes the solitary place the seat of God's church, and addresses the charge about weak hands to the ministers of God.

Henry sets this chapter beside the last: there a fruitful country was turned into a horrid wilderness, here a wilderness into good land; when the land was freed from the Assyrian army the ravaged districts began to recover, and when the Gentile nations, long a wilderness bringing forth no fruit to God, received the gospel, joy came with it.

debates.question: What flower is meant by the blossom of the desert?

positions.view: The narcissus, though primrose and crocus have been proposed.
Probably the crocus and primrose, which were classed together and are easily confounded, unlike narcissus and primrose.

debates.question: Who is told to strengthen the weak hands?

positions.view: The ministers of the word, as the following verse shows.
The prophet speaks; the words are his.
Whoever is addressed, the language is figurative, since the New Testament quotes it so.

outliers.note: Argues from the sublimity of the images themselves that their fulfilment must be extended past the first century to a later reign of the Messiah.

themes: The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.

It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing: the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it, the excellency of Carmel and Sharon, they shall see the glory of the Lord, and the excellency of our God.
Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees.
Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come with vengeance, even God with a recompence; he will come and save you.

5.pericope_label: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the word for the parched ground as what we now call the mirage, the sheen that looks like a sparkling lake and proves to be barren sand, and takes the promise to be that in place of the delusive show there shall be the lake itself; he corrects two words in the next clause, the creatures whose lair the desert was being better called jackals than dragons, and the grass better read as growing to the height of reeds and rushes. Delitzsch states the frame within which the miracles work, that amid them the people of God are redeemed and led home to Zion.

Gill says the words were literally fulfilled at the first coming of Christ and spiritually among Jews and Gentiles alike, especially under the apostles' ministry, when men blind in spiritual things had their understanding opened to see their own sinfulness and the suitableness of a Saviour; he reads the leaping of the lame the same way, of men impotent to any good who by the Spirit became able and willing, and applies the parched ground to men scorched with a sense of divine wrath and thirsting after grace. Calvin approaches the verse as the reversal of an earlier sentence, since the prophet probably alludes to his own former threatening of dreadful blindness and stupefaction of soul, and holds that we must come to Christ if we wish to know what these words mean; on the waters he builds a doctrine of provision, that there is no reason to dread want once we are reconciled to God through Christ, and that though wicked men often have great abundance their wealth is wretched, since they have not Christ, from whom alone a salutary abundance proceeds.

Clarke observes that the word for the parched ground is Arabic as well as Hebrew and means the same in both, the glowing sandy plain that at a distance looks like water; he quotes the Koran, where the works of unbelievers are like a vapour on a plain that the thirsty traveller takes for water until he comes and finds nothing, and a commentator's note that it means the false appearance seen on sandy plains about noon, a large lake in motion caused by the sun's beams on the quivering vapours. Wesley reads it all of the poor Gentiles, once blind and deaf, whose minds now have eyes and ears opened, and makes the dry places fruitful, meaning the effusion of God's grace on nations wholly destitute of it, noting that the reeds and rushes named grow only in moist ground.

Henry keeps the miracles bodily and lists them from the Gospels, sight given with a word to one born blind, the ears of the deaf unstopped by a single command, the lame given the use of their limbs; he sets them under wonders wrought in nature and grace together, sufficient to prove that it is no less than God who comes.

debates.question: Are the healings of the body or of the soul?

positions.view: Bodily, and wrought by Christ in the Gospels.
Both: literally at Christ's first coming, spiritually under the apostles' ministry.
Spiritual: the Gentiles, once blind and deaf, have the eyes and ears of their minds opened.
The reversal of an earlier sentence of blindness and stupefaction of soul, understood only in Christ.

debates.question: What is the parched ground that becomes a pool?

positions.view: The mirage: in place of a delusive sheen there shall be the lake itself.
The glowing sandy plain that looks like water from a distance, a word shared with Arabic and used so in the Koran.
Men scorched by divine wrath or by persecution, now comforted and refreshed.

outliers.note: Establishes the sense of a Hebrew word from Arabic usage and the Koran, quoting the parable of the unbeliever's works as a vapour on a plain.

themes: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.

8.pericope_label: And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness... And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the highway for a raised causeway and rejects the reading that refers it to the return of the exiles: it is rather the road by which the pilgrims of all nations shall journey to the mountain of the Lord's house, its name confirming that, a true sacred way to the earthly temple as a type of the eternal one not made with hands. He recalls that lions had not ceased to haunt the Jordan valley as in the days of the judges and early kings, and that the recent emptying of the northern kingdom had laid the country more open to them, and would render the second phrase not any ravenous beast but the most ravenous; on the redeemed and the ransomed he insists that the Hebrew words express simply release and freedom, without implying, as the English words do, a payment as their condition. He closes by saying the first volume of the prophecy ends fitly with a picture that carries thought beyond any earthly fulfilment, its imagery beginning perhaps from the processions of pilgrims singing at their halting-places, and that these are the closing words of the prophet's political activity, written probably in his old age. Delitzsch prints the last two verses together as the chapter's single closing movement.

Gill says the highway and the way are not two ways but one, a way cast up above the ground, and makes the road Christ himself, the only way of salvation; he takes the lions for wicked men, savage toward God's people, who once brought into this way become as tame as lambs, and keeps to the effect rather than the mechanism of redemption, the ransomed being turned from darkness to light and returned from straying to the Shepherd of souls. Calvin begins with the return from exile, promised so the exiles might not think themselves banished for ever, but extends it much farther, to places once uninhabited now filled with the journeys of a vast multitude and a land so at peace that men may pass without fear, since where there are no inhabitants there can be no roads; and he sets the absence of the lion against the curse of an earlier chapter, where wild beasts were to meet the Jews wherever they went, drawing the doctrine that God not only begins but carries through our salvation.

Clarke holds that the second word of the opening clause was added by mistake, sixteen manuscripts and three versions having it only once; where our version says the way shall be for those he would read that God himself shall be with them, walking in the way, the older English version having translated it so while the later translators were misled by the Jewish division of the sentence. On the redeemed and the ransomed he builds his reading on the idea of price, the first word meaning those whose forfeited inheritances are recovered by the kinsman, which he says all orthodox divines have referred to the incarnation and sacrifice of our Lord, and the second coming from a root meaning to redeem by paying a price. He ends on the sound of a single word, saying no sorrowful accent was ever better expressed than the strong guttural term used here for sighing, nearly the same as the cry of Irish funeral wailing. Wesley agrees that the highway and the way are one, a causeway that is raised earth and a road at once, and keeps the received sense that the road is for the weak and lame whom God will lead, and so plain that even the most foolish travellers cannot mistake it.

debates.question: Do the words for redeemed and ransomed imply a price paid?

positions.view: Yes, and that is the whole point: the kinsman recovering a forfeited inheritance, and a price paid down to release men from bondage.
No: the Hebrew words express simply release and freedom, without the payment the English words imply.
The effect matters more than the mechanism: the ransomed are turned from darkness to light.
To the mountain of the Lord's house, travelled by the pilgrims of all nations, not by returning exiles.
Home from exile first, but the promise extends much farther, to a land at peace and open to travel.
It is Christ himself, the only way of salvation.
It is for the weak and lame whom God leads, and too plain for even fools to mistake.

outliers.note: Rejects the received division of the sentence as an error taken over from Jewish authority, and would have God himself walking the road with his people.

themes: And an highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it; but it shall be for those: the wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.
No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon, it shall not be found there; but the redeemed shall walk there:
And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
